questions.q: Define situational irony and symbolism in your own words, giving one example of each from the story.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the outcome contradicts expectations: the Garoghlanian family, renowned for honesty for eleven centuries, has a cousin (Mourad) who steals a horse. Symbolism is using a concrete object to represent an abstract idea: the white horse symbolizes the boys' yearning for freedom and the purity of their tribe's ideals. A wrong answer (e.g., "irony is when something funny happens" or "the horse is just a horse") reveals the student confuses irony with coincidence/humour and treats symbols as literal plot objects only.

questions.q: Explain the dramatic irony in the scene where John Byro examines the horse's mouth and says, "Tooth for tooth... I would swear it is my horse if I didn't know your parents."
questions.a: Dramatic irony exists because the reader knows the boys stole the horse, while John Byro only suspects it; his statement acknowledges the physical evidence (the horse is identical) but deliberately overrides it with his knowledge of the family's reputation. A wrong answer (e.g., "John Byro is fooled" or "It's not irony because he knows") shows the student misses that Byro *chooses* to trust reputation over evidence — a subtle irony that protects the boys and the tribe's honour.

questions.q: Identify a symbol in the story other than the white horse. Explain what it represents and give one textual detail that supports your interpretation.
questions.a: The injured robin Mourad nurses represents the boys' own fragile innocence and their desire to nurture what is broken. Textual support: Mourad talks to the bird, repairs its wing, and throws it into the air where it "flew away, high and straight" — mirroring the boys' eventual return of the horse and their own moral flight. A wrong answer (e.g., "The barn is a symbol of hiding") without linking to theme shows the student picks random objects without thematic justification.

questions.q: Compare the situational irony of Mourad stealing the horse with the verbal irony in his statement: "What? he roared. Are you inviting a member of the Garoghlanian family to steal?"
questions.a: Situational irony: the tribe's honesty contrasts with the theft itself. Verbal irony: Mourad *has* stolen the horse, yet he roars at Aram for suggesting they keep it a year, pretending the very idea violates family honour. Both ironies work together — the situational irony sets up the moral conflict; the verbal irony reveals Mourad's self-deception and his desperate need to maintain the tribe's self-image. A wrong answer treating them as the same type or missing Mourad's performance shows the student cannot distinguish irony modes or see how they layer.

questions.q: Evaluate which is more central to the story's theme: the irony of the honest tribe stealing, or the symbolism of the white horse. Justify your choice with two textual reasons.
questions.a: The irony is more central because it structures the entire moral dilemma: the theft only matters *because* of the tribe's reputation (Uncle Khosrove's "It is no harm" vs. John Byro's loss). The horse's symbolism enriches the theme but the irony *drives* the plot and the boys' internal conflict. Textual reasons: (1) The opening establishes the tribe's honesty as "most important of all"; (2) The climax hinges on John Byro choosing the family's fame over his eyes. A wrong answer choosing symbolism without acknowledging the irony as the engine of the narrative shows the student prioritizes imagery over structural theme.

questions.q: Write a 4-sentence paragraph using situational irony and a symbol of your own invention to show a teenager's conflict between family expectations and personal desire.
questions.a: Expected answer: A paragraph where a teen from a family of doctors secretly applies to art school (situational irony: family pride vs. hidden rebellion) and uses a cracked sketchbook as a symbol of their damaged but persistent creativity. A poor answer (e.g., a simple narrative with no irony or a symbol used only literally) reveals the student cannot transfer the concepts to original writing — they only recognize devices, not wield them.
